transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-18
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Jin Park (Redwood SE), Ava Li (Redwood CSM); Tom Rivera (NebulaPay Backend), Priya Singh (NebulaPay ML Lead), Jared Cole (NebulaPay SRE), Lana Ortiz (NebulaPay PM)

Summary:
Quick recap of last week's run: steady-state plateau hit at ~1.8k rps with average gen latency 420ms, tail p95 980ms; identified burst-related queueing and under-utilized batching windows. Focus today: closed-loop adjustments to batching thresholds, concurrency target redefinition, and queue shaping knobs. Agree next forensic run and finalize pilot scale decision.

Topics:
- Continuous batching thresholds and auto-window sizing
- Concurrency caps vs queuing depth
- KV cache priming and impact on cold-start tails
- Fallback routing and burst smoothing
- Metrics / instrumentation to capture (per-batch tokens, unused slots, queue length)

Action items (light):
- SE to share heatmap and annotated runbook
- Customer to provide 7-day trace
- AE to share revised pilot cost projection

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): ok hi everyone, thanks for joining. quick check, is this still a good time for NebulaPay folks?
[00:07] Tom (NebulaPay): yeah yep all good, we have Priya and Jared on the line too. thanks for making time.
[00:12] Maya: awesome. we'll try to keep to 45 minutes, focus on the closed-loop tuning we discussed. Ethan, do you want to start with the run summary?
[00:21] Ethan (SE): sure. so from last week's 3 hour run, what stood out was the plateau around 1.7–1.9k rps for the 128 token average prompts. avg gen latency sat ~420ms but the p95 drifted up near the 1s mark during bursts. we instrumented per-batch occupancy—lots of partially filled batches during the low-variance periods, so we're not using the batching window efficiently. also noticed queue dwells when concurrency hit the cap, which then forced larger batches later and that spiked tails.
[00:50] Priya (ML Lead): do you think the KV cash impacts that? sometimes the first few requests after colder idle show big penalty.
[00:57] Ethan: yes KV cache (kv cache) priming was visible — cold sequence requests added ~80–120ms when the cache wasn't primed. but that's a smaller piece than the dynamic queuing we saw. tend to see the worst tails when small bursts push us past concurrency cap and then the runtime tries to batch aggressively.
[01:15] Jared (SRE): for context our traffic is spiky: daytime chunking with 5 minute microbursts every hour, plus a heavy nightly batch. We can fake a smoother distribution but want a config that handles native pattern.
[01:26] Jin (SE): that's helpful. so we want closed-loop control: adapt batch window based on running occupancy, but cap concurrency to avoid head-of-line blocking. idea is use a target occupancy ratio — e.g., 70–80% batch fill — and adjust batch delay window in small increments. when occupancy drops below threshold, increase wait-time by 5ms steps until we reach target, when occupancy is high, drop waiting.
[01:46] Priya: sounds reasonable, but isn't there a risk of added latency for single-request flows? some of our payments flows are single-turn and need <300ms.
[01:55] Ethan: right, so we plan to use request-level SLO tags. Redwood runtime can honor low-latency class: those requests bypass batching or get a minimal window. can we quantify how many of your calls are single-turn low-latency vs conversational?
[02:08] Tom: roughly 40% single-turn, 60% multi-turn, so we do need a hybrid approach.
[02:13] Maya: that's the reason we suggested an occupancy target per priority lane. low-latency lane concurrency set to 8, batch window 2ms; standard lane concurrency to 24 with adaptive window.
[02:24] Lana (PM): quick question: what's the practical difference between raising concurrency vs increasing batch windows? which gives us better throughput/cost?
[02:33] Ethan: raising concurrency increases parallelism but also increases memory pressure and can worsen kv cache eviction behavior; increasing batch window raises per-token efficiency but increases median latency. cost wins usually come from better batching efficiency — fewer small batches means lower GPU kernel overhead — but you pay in latency. It's tradeoff.
[02:51] Priya: can we simulate cost delta? like if we push avg batch fill from 55% to 80% what happens to tokens/cost?
[02:58] Jin: yes we have a micro-sim. rough ballpark: going from 55 to 80 fills saved ~18% token-equivalent overhead in our test model for 512 context. we'll share the simulation sheet.
[03:11] Maya: action: SE - drop simulation link into chat.
[03:15] Jin: noted. share after.
[03:17] [03:20] Jared: another thing — our p95 spikes correlate with burst handoff from our API gateway. When gateway pushes a 200 req spike we go from 10rps to 900rps in 400ms window. that kills concurrency smoothing.
[03:34] Ethan: in that case we recommend two-pronged approach: gateway rate-smoothing (token-bucket on your side) plus runtime queue shaping on our side. runtime queue shaping means limiting inflight per-model and using a small ingress queue with tail-drop + burst tokens. That plus prioritized lanes for critical paths should smooth tails.
[03:51] Tom: we can add a small smoothing buffer upstream (we have a request buffer in front of the LB). but want Redwood to be resilient w/o heavy infra changes.
[03:59] Ethan: we can do that — we'll tweak queue size and burst allowance. we also have fallback routing to a lower-cost sharded replica — it decompresses throughput but with slightly higher median latency; useful if we see capacity pressure.
[04:13] Priya: when you say fallback replica, you mean a smaller model variant? or a model hosted in another cluster?
[04:18] Jin: variant or different instance size — e.g. quantized Llama-2 13b variant vs full 13b fp16. fallback trades quality for capacity. we can also route to dedicated reserved pool if you're on Dedicated.
[04:31] Maya: quick check on NebulaPay's constraints — Priya? do you have any data residency or encryption blockers for routing?
[04:38] Priya: no residency issues, just strict audit and SSO. but routing across cloud regions is fine.
[04:43] Maya: good.
[04:44] [05:00] Ethan: i've prepared a proposed tuning set for this week:
- set standard lane concurrency hard cap to 24 (was 16)
- adaptive batch window starting at 6ms, step +/- 3ms based on occupancy, target 75%
- ingress queue depth 400 with burst tokens 120
- low-latency lane concurrency 8, batch window 2ms, max wait 6ms
- KV cache pre-warm script for warm-starts during test runs

[05:33] Tom: curious—how did you pick 24? we're worried about memory per-worker.
[05:38] Jin: 24 is based on our CPU/GPU profiling on your model variant with 512 context; it keeps memory headroom while increasing kernel utilization. if memory becomes an issue we can reduce concurrency and raise batch window.
[05:50] Jared: question: does increasing concurrency mean more processes or higher threads within process? how does that impact OOMs?
[05:58] Ethan: it's more slots per worker, runtime handles continuous batching. so memory impact is roughly linear with in-flight KV caches and KV store per slot. that's why we limit low-latency lane to keep footprint small.
[06:10] Priya: okay. also earlier you said unused batch slots were high — can you explain cause?
[06:16] Ethan: mostly due to mismatch: the batch scheduler opens a window expecting fills, but requests are sparse in parts of your traffic. so you get many partially filled batches. closed-loop control reacts by widening window which increases fill, but if widen too much latency increases. goal is to find sweet spot.
[06:33] Maya: totally. the closed-loop algorithm we'll deploy runs with small epsilon adjustments and has safety bounds so it won't blow latency. We'll push it in canary first.
[06:40] Lana: can you describe the canary? what percentage traffic and how you measure regressions?
[06:45] Jin: recommended canary: 5–10% of traffic for 4 hours during high-variance window. primary metrics: p50, p95, p99 gen latency, avg batch fill, GPU utilization, and per-batch tokens. abort if p95 increases >15% or error rate increases >0.2%.
[07:03] Tom: seems fine. we want to avoid any visible applicative errors to users.
[07:07] Maya: agreed. we'll include circuit-breaker to revert live.
[07:10] [07:20] Priya: about KV cache priming — will the pre-warm script run per-model or per-customer? we multi-tenant the pool now.
[07:26] Ethan: can be per-customer keying — we can prime keyspaces for NebulaPay on the dedicated pool; in hosted we can tag requests so the runtime keeps a hot partition for you. that helps cold-start p95.
[07:38] Jared: is there a way to see kv eviction logs? would help us correlate.
[07:42] Jin: yes we'll enable kv eviction metrics from the runtime and push them to your prometheus endpoint. also export per-run batch occupancy histograms.
[07:52] Tom: excellent.
[07:54] [08:10] Maya: quick pause — is anyone blocked on infra changes before we flip the canary?
[08:15] Tom: we need to add the upstream smoothing buffer (two small token-buckets) but can do that tonight. we'll also pull a 7 day trace for you.
[08:23] Priya: we'll run a 6-hour steady-state bench tomorrow night to capture the nighttime batch pattern.
[08:29] Maya: perfect. so the SEs will push the config and scripts; NebulaPay runs bench and share traces; AE sends cost projection.
[08:36] [08:40] Ethan: i want to call out one subtlety — during one of the test runs we saw 'batch re-ordering' when fallbacks triggered: when a request was rerouted to fallback replica, we lost ordering and some session continuations saw mismatched KV contexts. we fixed this by pinning session affinity for fallback flows. just flagging so Priya knows.
[09:02] Priya: thanks — we'll look for that in logs.
[09:06] Jin: also note the runtime now supports 'session-affinity tokens' which we can attach. it's small change in request headers.
[09:13] Tom: ok we'll add header sidecar.
[09:16] [09:30] Maya: let's surface what success looks like for the next run. Priya?
[09:35] Priya: aim: p95 <650ms, stable p99 under 1.4s, average batch fill >70%, and no increase in error rate. If we hit that for the 6-hour bench we feel good to scale pilot.
[09:49] Ethan: to add, target cost per 1k queries should not exceed last week's baseline by more than 8% — we want net efficiency.
[09:57] Lana: and product will sign off if there are no user-facing regressions.
[10:01] [10:20] Maya: timeline and responsibilities:
- Today: SEs push adaptive tuning scripts and share playbook (Ethan, Jin)
- Tomorrow: NebulaPay runs 6-hour steady-state overnight bench (Tom, Jared)
- Thu: SEs ingest logs and share per-batch heatmap + annotated findings (Ethan)
- Fri: AE shares pilot cost projection and recommended next-step scale plan (Maya)

[10:44] Tom: will you share a short checklist for the bench so we capture everything? CPU/GPU counters, batch occupancy, lat histograms, and kv eviction traces?
[10:53] Ethan: yes a bench checklist will be in the runbook. we'll include curl examples with session-affinity tokens and a Grafana dashboard link.
[10:59] [11:20] Priya: small nit — the runtime logs sometimes mis-label model names in traces (we saw 'red-13b' vs 'neb-13b') — not a blocker but makes correlation messy. can you normalize naming?
[11:32] Jin: yes that's logging mapping; we'll add a tag for 'nebulapay:model:v1' so your traces match.
[11:38] Jared: also, is metric cardinality going to explode if you add session tags? keep that in mind.
[11:44] Ethan: good point — we'll use hashed session id and sampling for traces to keep cardinality bounded.
[11:50] [12:00] Maya: any other risks?
[12:03] Lana: just stakeholder alignment on cost. we want clear delta.
[12:07] Maya: we'll include a conservative and optimistic cost scenario in the projection.
[12:10] Tom: one last ask — can Redwood run a short-endurance test to validate fallback routing behavior? maybe 15 minutes of forced overload?
[12:19] Ethan: yes we can run an overload test in our staging and provide the script. we'll coordinate times.
[12:24] [12:40] Priya: ok good.
[12:42] Maya: great — recap of next steps in chat. thanks all.
[12:47] Tom: thanks everyone.
[12:49] Jin: thanks.
[12:50] Maya: bye.
